ph-and-solubility-s1.title: Five slightly soluble salts
ph-and-solubility-s1.text: Each salt dissolves only slightly in pure water at 25 °C. Ka values are given for the conjugate acid of each anion; "strong" means the conjugate acid is a strong acid.

table.caption: Salts and the acid each anion comes from
rows: (OH⁻ reacts with H₃O⁺ to make water)

ph-and-solubility-s2.title: Calcium fluoride in water and in acid
ph-and-solubility-s2.html: Key: Ca²⁺ calcium ion; F⁻ fluoride; HF hydrogen fluoride molecule; H₃O⁺ hydronium. Each box is the solution above undissolved CaF₂(s), not drawn, at the same temperature. Water and the anions of the added acid are not drawn.

ph-and-solubility-s3.title: Dissolving a hydroxide
ph-and-solubility-s3.text:
Three test tubes each contain 0.10 g of solid Mg(OH)₂ in 10 mL of liquid: Tube A, distilled water; Tube B, 1.0 M HCl; Tube C, 1.0 M NaOH. The tubes are shaken and left to settle.

Mg(OH)₂(s) ⇌ Mg²⁺(aq) + 2 OH⁻(aq)

items.q: Which salts become more soluble when the solution is made more acidic? Select all that apply.
options: CaF₂
AgCl
BaCO₃
PbI₂
Mg(OH)₂

why.correct: Each of these anions is a base: H₃O⁺ converts F⁻ to HF, CO₃²⁻ to HCO₃⁻ (and on to H₂CO₃ and CO₂), and OH⁻ to water. Removing the anion makes Q < Ksp, so more solid dissolves.
options: Right: F⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HF.
Cl⁻ comes from a strong acid and does not react with H₃O⁺.
Right: carbonate is a fairly strong base.
I⁻ comes from a strong acid and does not react with H₃O⁺.
Right: H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2 H₂O removes hydroxide.

items.q: Which explanation correctly says why adding HNO₃ dissolves more CaF₂(s)?
options: H₃O⁺ turns F⁻ into HF, so Q < Ksp
HNO₃ increases the Ksp of the CaF₂ solid
NO₃⁻ ions react with Ca²⁺ to form a soluble compound
The H₃O⁺ ions attack the solid and break its covalent bonds

why.correct: The answer names the reaction (F⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HF + H₂O), its effect on Q, and the shift: the reasoning readers look for.
options: Right: Q vs Ksp with the specific reaction.
Ksp depends only on temperature; it is Q that changes.
Calcium nitrate is soluble, but NO₃⁻ was not needed to remove Ca²⁺; the effect comes from removing F⁻.
CaF₂ is an ionic solid; dissolving separates ions rather than breaking covalent bonds.

items.q: How does adding HNO₃ change the solubility of AgCl?
options: Very little: Cl⁻ does not react with H₃O⁺
It increases, because H₃O⁺ reacts with Cl⁻ to form HCl
It decreases, because NO₃⁻ is a common ion
It increases, because salts dissolve better in acid

why.correct: HCl is a strong acid, so Cl⁻ has essentially no tendency to take a proton. [Cl⁻] stays the same, Q is unchanged, and the solubility is unchanged.
options: Right: no reaction with the anion, no shift.
HCl would immediately ionize again; Cl⁻ is not removed.
NO₃⁻ is not in AgCl, so it is not a common ion.
Only salts whose anions are bases dissolve better in acid.

items.q: Of CaF₂ and BaCO₃, whose solubility rises more sharply as pH is lowered from 7 to 5, and why?
options: BaCO₃: CO₃²⁻ is the stronger base
CaF₂, because HF has the larger Ka
Both equally, because both anions are bases
CaF₂, because it releases two anions per formula unit

why.correct: The Ka of HCO₃⁻ (4.7 × 10⁻¹¹) is far smaller than that of HF (6.8 × 10⁻⁴), so CO₃²⁻ is a far stronger base: at pH 5–7 nearly all of it is protonated, while F⁻ (pKa 3.17) is still mostly unprotonated at pH 5.
options: Right: the weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base and the bigger the pH effect.
A larger Ka means F⁻ is the weaker base, so it is protonated less.
Both are bases, but of very different strength.
The number of anions matters for Ksp, but the pH effect depends on how readily the anion takes a proton.

items.q: Which box best represents the solution after a strong acid is added to Box 1 and equilibrium is restored?
options: Box 2
Box 3
Box 4
Box 1, unchanged

why.correct: More CaF₂ dissolved (4 Ca²⁺ instead of 1), and most of its fluoride became HF. F atoms are conserved (1 F⁻ + 7 HF = 8 = 2 × 4 Ca²⁺), and the free-ion product [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² is 4 × 1² = 4, the same as Box 1 (1 × 2² = 4), as Ksp requires.
options: Right: more dissolved, fluoride mostly protonated, ion product back at Ksp.
Box 3 shows more dissolved with no HF: its ion product (4 × 8² = 256) is far above Ksp, so it is not at equilibrium.
Box 4 has no free F⁻, so Q = 0 < Ksp: more solid would still dissolve. It is not at equilibrium.
Adding acid removes F⁻, so the solution cannot stay the same.

items.q: In every box, the total number of F atoms (in F⁻ and HF) should be twice the number of Ca²⁺ ions. Why?
options: Both come from CaF₂, with two F per Ca
Ca²⁺ has a 2+ charge, so it attracts two water molecules
HF molecules contain two atoms
Ksp has [F⁻] squared

why.correct: Dissolving CaF₂ releases one Ca²⁺ and two F⁻; protonating F⁻ to HF does not change the number of F atoms.
options: Right: the formula sets the ratio.
The ratio comes from the formula of the salt, not from hydration.
The number of atoms in HF does not set the Ca : F ratio.
The square in Ksp follows from the same formula; it is a consequence, not the cause.

items.q: A strong acid is added to the saturated CaF₂ solution with solid present. Predict the change in each once equilibrium is restored.

variables.name: Mass of CaF₂(s) remaining
variables.why: Removing F⁻ makes Q < Ksp, so more solid dissolves.

variables.name: [Ca²⁺]
variables.why: More CaF₂ dissolves, releasing more Ca²⁺.

why.correct: The acid removes the basic anion, and the dissolving equilibrium shifts right to replace it.

items.q: A student claims, "Adding acid dissolves CaF₂ because the acid raises Ksp." Which evidence from Boxes 1 and 2 contradicts the claim?
options: [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² is equal in both boxes
Box 2 contains more Ca²⁺ than Box 1
Box 2 contains HF molecules
Box 1 contains no H₃O⁺ ions

why.correct: Box 1: 1 × 2² = 4; Box 2: 4 × 1² = 4. The free-ion product, which equals Ksp at equilibrium, did not change. More salt dissolved because acid hid most of the fluoride as HF.
options: Right: Ksp is unchanged; the extra dissolving comes from removing F⁻.
More Ca²⁺ shows that more salt dissolved, which fits either explanation.
HF shows that F⁻ reacted, but on its own does not test the claim about Ksp.
This describes the starting state, not the effect of the acid.

items.q: In which tube does the most Mg(OH)₂ dissolve?
options: Tube B
Tube A
Tube C
The same amount in each

why.correct: H₃O⁺ in HCl reacts with OH⁻ (H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2 H₂O), driving [OH⁻] down, so the dissolving equilibrium shifts right until the solid dissolves.
options: Right: acid removes OH⁻.
Water dissolves only a trace of Mg(OH)₂.
Added OH⁻ is a common ion; it pushes the equilibrium left.
The liquids affect [OH⁻] very differently.

items.q: Why does even less Mg(OH)₂ dissolve in Tube C than in Tube A?
options: OH⁻ is a common ion, so Q reaches Ksp sooner
NaOH reacts with Mg(OH)₂ to form a new solid
Na⁺ ions lower Ksp
NaOH raises the temperature

why.correct: The large [OH⁻] makes Q = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]² exceed Ksp at a tiny [Mg²⁺], so the dissolving stops much earlier.
options: Right: the common-ion effect.
No new solid is involved; the effect is on Q.
Ksp does not change with added ions.
Dissolving a little NaOH in 10 mL does warm it slightly, but that is not why the solubility falls.

items.q: Put the steps of the explanation for Tube B in order.
options: HCl supplies H₃O⁺
H₃O⁺ reacts with OH⁻ to form water
[OH⁻] falls, so Q = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]² < Ksp
The net dissolving reaction proceeds until Q = Ksp again, so more solid dissolves

why.correct: Source of acid, the reaction that removes the anion, the effect on Q compared with Ksp, then the shift. This is the claim-evidence-reasoning chain readers want.

items.q: A student repeats Tube B with 1.0 M NaCl instead of 1.0 M HCl. What result is expected?
options: About as little as in water: NaCl adds no H₃O⁺
As much dissolves as in HCl, because both contain Cl⁻
More dissolves than in HCl, because Na⁺ reacts with OH⁻
Nothing dissolves, because Cl⁻ is a common ion

why.correct: The effect in Tube B came from H₃O⁺. NaCl solution is neutral, and neither Na⁺ nor Cl⁻ reacts with Mg²⁺ or OH⁻, so the result is like water. This control shows the acid, not the chloride, was responsible.
options: Right: it isolates H₃O⁺ as the cause.
Cl⁻ was a spectator in Tube B.
NaOH is soluble; Na⁺ does not remove OH⁻.
Cl⁻ is not part of Mg(OH)₂, so it is not a common ion.

items.q: Tooth enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, Ca₅(PO₄)₃OH. Why do acidic drinks wear it away?
options: H₃O⁺ removes its OH⁻ and PO₄³⁻ ions
Acid raises the Ksp of hydroxyapatite
Acid adds Ca²⁺, a common ion, to the enamel
Acid makes the phosphate ions larger and looser

why.correct: OH⁻ and PO₄³⁻ are both bases. H₃O⁺ removes them, Q drops below Ksp, and enamel dissolves.
options: Right: basic anions are removed by acid.
Ksp changes only with temperature.
Drinks do not add Ca²⁺ in this explanation, and a common ion would lower solubility.
Ion size is not changed by acid.

items.q: For which salts would adding NaOH (raising the pH) have little effect on solubility through acid-base reactions? Select all that apply.
options: AgBr
Ca₃(PO₄)₂
BaSO₄
ZnCO₃
Fe(OH)₂

why.correct: Raising the pH removes nothing from salts whose ions do not react with OH⁻. Br⁻ and SO₄²⁻ are very weak bases and do not react with OH⁻ either. (Phosphate and carbonate salts become, if anything, less soluble as pH rises, because their anions stay unprotonated.)
options: Right: Br⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid.
Phosphate salts are strongly affected by pH: they dissolve in acid, and raising the pH reverses that.
Right: SO₄²⁻ is a very weak base, so its salts are hardly affected by pH.
Carbonate salts are strongly pH dependent.
Adding OH⁻ to a hydroxide salt is a common-ion effect: it lowers the solubility.

items.q: Which claim about pH and solubility is correct?
options: A salt with a basic anion dissolves more at lower pH
Any salt dissolves more as pH decreases
A salt becomes more soluble as pH decreases because acid increases Ksp
A salt with a strong-acid anion becomes more soluble as pH increases

why.correct: Only basic anions (F⁻, CO₃²⁻, PO₄³⁻, OH⁻, S²⁻ and similar) react with H₃O⁺; that reaction is what shifts the dissolving equilibrium.
options: Right: the anion must be a base.
Salts of Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ and NO₃⁻ are unaffected by pH.
Ksp does not change; Q does.
Anions from strong acids are unaffected by pH in either direction.
